name: Romantic Period
description: Literature written in British and American English between the French Revolution and the first British Reform Act. In Britain: the great generation of Wordsworth, Coleridge, Blake, Byron, Shelley and Keats; the novels of Austen, Scott and Edgeworth; the philosophical tale of Godwin and Mary Shelley; the high Gothic of Radcliffe, Lewis and Maturin; the ballad revival and the literary annual; and the prose of Hazlitt, Lamb and De Quincey. In America: the gothic tales of Charles Brockden Brown, Bryant's nature lyric, Washington Irving's sketches, Cooper's romance of the forest and the sea, and the sermon, review and dictionary culture of the new republic.
historical_context: The period opens with the fall of the Bastille (1789) and closes with the Great Reform Act (1832). Between those dates: the revolutionary and Napoleonic wars and the British repressions of 1792-1815; the Act of Union with Ireland (1800); the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade by Britain and by the United States (1807-1808); the Congress system after Waterloo (1815); Peterloo (1819), the Six Acts and the Cato Street conspiracy; Catholic emancipation (1829). Economically: enclosure, the Corn Laws (1815), factory labour, the depression of 1815-1821, and the expansion of the provincial and London press. In the United States: the Federalist and Republican contest, the Louisiana Purchase (1803), the War of 1812, the Missouri Compromise (1820), and the election of Andrew Jackson (1828).
literary_characteristics: A literature of the imagination, of solitary and meditative selfhood, and of revolution in its hopes and in its disappointments. Verse abandons the closed heroic couplet for blank verse, the conversation poem, the hymn, the ballad, the ode and the sonnet; the supernatural, the ruined castle, the mountain and the ocean become serious subjects. Prose fiction divides into the philosophical and anarchistic tale, the romance of terror, the Scottish historical novel, the novel of manners, and the American romance of forest and coast. Criticism becomes professional and review-bound (Edinburgh, Quarterly, Blackwood's, the North American Review); the annual and the keepsake create a new market for verse and the short tale. The familiar essay develops a modern prose of memory and self-analysis.
